title: Book 6 — Erato, Chapter 52
paragraphs: For the Lacedaemonians, who on this matter agree with none of the poets, say that Aristodemus son of Aristomachus, son of Cleodaeus, son of Hyllus, being their king, himself led them (and not the sons of Aristodemus) to this land which they now possess. Then, not long afterward, the wife of Aristodemus, whose name was Argeia—she was the daughter, they say, of Autesion son of Tisamenus son of Thersander son of Polyneices—is said to have borne twins; and Aristodemus lived only long enough to see his children, and then ended his life by sickness. The Lacedaemonians of that time resolved, according to established custom, to make the elder of the children their king; but they did not know which of them they should take, because they were alike and of equal size. When they were unable to find out, or even before this, they inquired of their mother; but she said that even she herself did not know one from the other. This she said, although she actually knew quite well, because she desired that somehow both might be made kings. The Lacedaemonians were therefore in a difficulty; and being in a difficulty, they sent to Delphi to ask what they should do in the matter. The Pythian priestess bade them regard both children as their kings, but honor most the first in age. So, they say, did the priestess give them her answer; and when the Lacedaemonians were no less at a loss how to find out the elder of them, a Messenian named Panites made a suggestion to them. This Panites, I say, suggested to the Lacedaemonians that they watch the mother and see which of the children she washed and fed first of the two; and if she was seen to do this always in the same order, they would have all they were seeking and wished to discover; but if she too was uncertain and did it in a different order at different times, it would be plain to them that she had no more knowledge than anyone else, and they must turn to some other way. The Spartans, following the Messenian's suggestion, watched the mother of the sons of Aristodemus and found that she gave preference thus to the firstborn, both in feeding and in washing, not knowing she was being watched. They therefore took the child honored by its mother and brought it up in the public hall as the firstborn, and named it Eurysthenes; and the other was called Procles. When they had grown up, both of them, they say, were at variance with one another throughout their whole lives, although they were brothers, and their descendants continued in the same way.
